name: Heavy items on high shelves

6-12m.rationale: Pulling up begins; a child can reach low shelves first. No age-split evidence, so scored conservatively.

12-24m.rationale: Climbing and pulling on shelves and furniture; AAP warns children can be seriously hurt pulling on heavy furniture.

24-36m.rationale: Climbers use shelves as steps; scored conservatively.

injury_evidence.cause_category: shelving and bookcase tip-over (related, not the same as items falling from shelves)
injury_evidence.note: CPSC 2023 tip-over report (Feb 2024): of about 6,400 annual average ER-treated furniture tip-over injuries to children, 2020-2022, shelving and bookcases were about 1,000 (16%). This counts the furniture tipping, not objects falling off shelves, so it supports the topic only indirectly. No figure for items falling from high shelves was found.

why_it_matters: Children pull and climb, and a heavy object pulled or knocked off a shelf can fall on them. Moving heavy items low and out of reach, and anchoring shelves, reduces the risk.

fix_steps.text: Move heavy and breakable items (computers, large books, glass) to lower, rear positions that a child cannot reach, or out of the room.
Put lightweight items on the shelves a child can reach and keep cords from lamps and devices out of reach.
Anchor bookcases and shelving to the wall with brackets or straps.
Teach older children not to climb on shelves or use drawers as steps.

verify_rule: Nothing heavy sits on a shelf or surface a child can reach, and shelving is anchored to the wall.
blind_spots: Weight of objects (a photo shows size, not weight)
Whether a shelf is anchored to a stud
Shelves in other rooms or relatives' homes
